title: Culture Vultures
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Shaun Brien, a Victorian teacher and learning specialist, examines what creates staff culture in schools during a teacher shortage in which staff can easily jump ship. He is sceptical of a keynote that urged schools to be more roundabout than traffic light, arguing that grey areas breed distrust when staff are treated differently. He contrasts the anything-goes school, which drives workload and fragmentation, with the micromanaged school, which breeds malicious compliance. His answer is psychological safety and leadership that models what it asks, illustrated by his own successful push to fix pointless staff meetings, and he insists culture does not come from pizza parties.
points: Staff culture, defined as the collective views and values of teachers, is hard to maintain when a shortage lets teachers leave and schools hire anyone available.
Grey areas in policy create perceived unfairness and distrust, which argues against an overly flexible roundabout model of school leadership.
Both extremes fail: anything-goes autonomy fragments curriculum and inflates workload, while perceived micromanagement produces malicious compliance and turnover.
Psychological safety to question leaders lets staff buy in because they feel ownership of decisions.
Culture is set from the top, and leaders who do not practise a school priority signal it does not matter.
quotes: All of the above has created a scenario where staff culture can be difficult to maintain. For the purpose of this piece of writing I’m defining staff culture as the collective views and values of teachers within a school.

If there’s anything I’ve experienced within schools that can create distrust and long term problems it is grey area. Grey area can very quickly be misinterpreted as different staff members get treated differently based on similar situations when there is no hard and fast process which should be followed.

The main issue with a school which is believed to micromanage staff is that it creates a degree of distrust between staff and leadership and can lead to malicious compliance occurring where staff only do the minimum required to not have leadership follow up with them.

Psychological safety here is really referring to the idea that an individual feels safe speaking their opinions without fear of reprisal or punishment. Realistically, all teaching staff should feel some level of psychological safety if they are on an ongoing contract as their job remains safe unless they infringe on a very serious law.

So if staff feel safe to speak up and voice their concerns, they’re more likely to feel valued and therefore buy in to school initiatives as they have more ownership of the decisions made along the way. Staff culture doesn’t come from pizza parties, Friday night drinks, trivia nights etc.
Culture also comes from the top. If staff see that leadership are not practicing what they preach then the trust is instantly gone.

I told her that questioning things that conflict with your internal beliefs is good, because it means that you’re not simply willing to follow whatever you are told to do and want to makes sure that evidence supports it. Everyone should feel safe to question things in their jobs because if staff are unsure they’re unlikely to fully support anything and that’s where culture dies a slow death.
